title: How To Actually Apply 'High Expectations'
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that 'high expectations' has become an empty slogan in education -- everyone nods along to its importance without a workable definition of what it actually requires in daily practice. He proposes a specific operational definition: for teachers, it means every lesson taught must be proven by students performing it independently, which places the burden of quality on the clarity and rigor of instruction itself. For students, it means that once something is taught, only they can do the work of mastering it -- no amount of teacher handholding substitutes for that. He directly rebuts the objection that this standard is unrealistic for struggling or disadvantaged students, calling the belief that certain students 'can't do it' a harmful lie that effectively excuses low performance, and links it to national reading and math proficiency failures. The piece is framed as a corrective to vague aspirational language, insisting that real improvement only follows once expectations are defined precisely enough to change what happens lesson by lesson.
points: Redefines high expectations concretely: every taught lesson must be proven through independent student performance, not just teacher intention.
Places responsibility on lesson quality first -- if lessons are exceptional, independent mastery becomes achievable for students.
Rejects the idea that struggling students, difficult schools, or 'low performers' are exceptions to this standard as a harmful, self-fulfilling excuse.
Links vague, undefined high-expectations rhetoric to real outcomes, citing roughly 75 percent of eighth graders failing to read or do math proficiently.
quotes: The importance of having high expectations for students is thrown about so often that it’s lost any real meaning.
For high expectations to mean anything at all, there must be a clear target and a path to get there.

For teachers, high expectations means that everything you teach must be proven by students independently. Therefore, for students to be able to do the work as taught, your lessons need to be exceptional.
For students, high expectations means that everything that is taught must be then performed all on their own.
Forgive me, but this is a lie from the pit of Gehanna and the reason nearly 75 percent of eighth graders can’t read or do math proficiently.
The truth is, they can do it, all of them and at a high level. But you have to expect it in the true sense and practice of the word, one lesson at a time.
